title: Powerful Conversations
description: Sometimes great communication with your leader may come naturally (if it does, great!). Other times it may be a challenge, especially if your leader has a different personality type or communication style than you do. As a female leader, there are a few things you can do to optimize interactions with your leader.

blocks.markdown: When it comes to being a female leader, nothing can make or break your career quite like communication, especially communication with your leader. Many times a female leader is reporting to a supervisor of the opposite sex—or maybe you’re managing team members of the opposite sex, making the communication gap even trickier. While we won’t go into all the nuances of male-female communications here, there are a few practical things you can do to make sure your communication is received in the best possible light, especially when it comes to communicating with your leader, having difficult conversations, and negotiating successfully, which we’ll cover in the following lesson.

Sometimes great communication with your leader may come naturally (if it does, great!). Other times it may be a challenge, especially if your leader has a different personality type or communication style than you do. As a female leader, there are a few things you can do to optimize interactions with your leader.

Know your leader's communication style. This can be summed up in three parts:

sections.title: Right timing
sections.body: Right timing

sections.title: How often do they prefer communications?
sections.body: How often do they prefer communications? Leaders are busy, and some managers prefer frequent updates, while some prefer consolidated updates. Some prefer to receive news/information as it happens in real time, while some prefer to hold items to be discussed in a one-on-one or meeting. Take a minute to think about your leader’s overall preferences. (When in doubt, just ask them!)

sections.title: Make sure your communication is professional, concise, and free from frustration.
sections.body: Make sure your communication is professional, concise, and free from frustration. More on this later.

sections.body:
In review, here are some of the ways we've suggested to sustain an open and communicative environment with your leader:
Optimize Your 1:1s
Be positive
Be prepared
Bring solutions
Be open to feedback

sections.title: Optimize your 1:1s with your leader.
sections.body: Optimize your 1:1s with your leader.

sections.title: Don’t overlook the rapport that can be formed in regular one-on-ones with your leader.
sections.body: Don’t overlook the rapport that can be formed in regular one-on-ones with your leader. Many times this is the foundation for trust that will help your career sink or swim.

sections.title: Be Positive
sections.body: Be Positive

sections.title: This should be a given, but it’s not.
sections.body:
This should be a given, but it’s not. Employees who bring a sense of positivity to work are rarer than you think, and in the world of leadership it can be a breath of fresh air. It doesn’t matter how talented you are—if your attitude is negative (or perceived as negative), your relationship with your leader will eventually suffer. Make positivity a part of your personal brand. Not all conversations will be positive in themselves, but when faced with something negative to communicate, try your best to frame it in a positive way.
“No one ever got anywhere, accomplished anything, or survived any amount of ill luck by being negative… With attitude you can determine your own performance.”
– Pat Summitt

sections.title: Be Prepared
sections.body: Be Prepared

sections.title: A little preparation goes a long way.
sections.body: A little preparation goes a long way. Whenever you take up your leader’s time, even in a standing meeting or one-on-one, come prepared with a list of items to discuss or an agenda for the meeting, in addition to any information or data that may be needed.

sections.title: Bring Solutions
sections.body: Bring Solutions

sections.title: This one is important!
sections.body: This one is important! Leaders often feel like their office is a revolving door of problems to solve. Whenever bringing an issue to your leader, also present some options for solving the problem. Your leader may have thoughts of their own on the matter, but the fact that you took the time to think through solutions will go a long way in displaying your own leadership abilities. Depending on the issue and vantage point, sometimes you may be even more qualified to solve the problem than your leader.

sections.title: Be Open to Feedback
sections.body: Be Open to Feedback

sections.title: Finally, be open to feedback and take any constructive criticism with an open mind.
sections.body:
Finally, be open to feedback and take any constructive criticism with an open mind. Remember, there’s usually a grain of truth in every bit of feedback, even if the feedback seems severe at the time.
Giving feedback is a sign of respect and care. Your leader cares enough to offer it to you and believes you have the maturity to receive it. Try not to get defensive about critiques or criticism, but instead use it to propel your best work forward.

questions.prompt: Which are an important part of knowing your leader’s communication style, or the “three rights” discussed in this lesson?

choices.text: Right tone, right posture, right gestures
Right place, right people, right feedback
Right channel, right timing, right message

questions.prompt: How can you optimize your 1:1s with your leader?
When presenting a problem to your leader, why is it important to provide solutions?

choices.text: Your leader probably can’t solve the issue on their own.
Thinking through solutions is a key leadership quality.
Leaders rarely have any problems to solve.
It shows that you are smarter than your colleagues.
